title: Duh - finally leaving fin advisor… how, what next?
body:
O.P.
For the last 15+ years I have been paying a financial advisor to ‘manage my affairs’. Before I was with him, I had a fair amount in Australian Super but he eventually moved me out of that and into managed funds plus cash.
Last financial year my total fees and costs were $23.8k made up of: $10.5k – advisor; $2k Macquarie; $10.8k fund fees. Ugh – and that’s only last year!
Thanks to a friend, my accountant and ChatGPT I have now woken up to the price I’ve paid for someone to soothe my fears and overwhelm around money – and ready to step up to DIY.
I’m 62, working part-time for myself (currently income = expenses). I’d be really grateful for any advice on how to transition most effectively to a safe, simple, easy to manage system – maybe an industry fund and eventually TTR? Would love some ideas. Do I need to think about tax implications?
Btw after I told my advisor I would not be renewing our agreement, he sent me an email saying he was restructuring his business and could now offer me a discount as I was one of his oldest customers! I won’t be taking up that offer.
Here is my current financial situation:
Macquarie Super Consolidator II – Elevate
Aust Listed Securities : $188,000 Vanguard Ethically Conscious AU
Managed Funds: $131,000 Aust Ethical Share $103,000 Loftus Peak Global Disruption $294,000 Vanguard Ethically Conscious $138,000 Hyperion Global Growth
Cash: $93,000 Macquarie Wrap Consolidated $620,000 Macquarie Term Deposits (just matured – not sure if they have automatically rolled over)
My advisor told me that I can’t keep the managed funds without him on my Macquarie account as my advisor. So I don’t think I can remove him until I have transitioned out of those funds.
Thanks in advance for any ideas, wisdom :)

[User #1247826180 postsbentlegyep, they are all bentWhirlpool Forums Addict] What is the status of your superannuation?
Are you contributing to Super?
How much inside and how much outside of Super?
[User #4670893279 postsflywireWhirlpool Forums Addict] this post was edited
If you've ever left a job (even years ago), you'd meet a condition of release at 62 since you're over 60. Specifically, "ceasing an employment arrangement on or after age 60," allowing full super access without permanent retirement declaration or hour limits on your employment.
I understand you can't do an in-specie rollover, so starting the pension first lets you sell tax-free, then rollover the cash proceeds tax-free to another fund. Selling assets inside Macquarie Super after starting a full retirement pension (not TTR) incurs zero CGT, as pension phase assets are CGT-exempt, while accumulation phase sales hit 15% (10% effective >12 months).

[User #480982176 postsCharlieCIt's a dog's lifeParticipant] I’ve just been through the same and was with Macquarie Wrap and with investments that required me to have a FA. So I had no choice but to sell everything down once I decided to dispense with an FA. I’m 64 and met the condition of release. Macquarie allowed an In specie transfer to roll everything into Pension mode before selling down. This avoided what could have been a costly CGT charge because the sell down happened in Pension mode where you don’t pay CGT. . Then the cash was rolled back to an accumulation account to allow me to move it to another fund. I selected an industry fund, HostPlus and am in a mix of balanced and growth with about 3 years of cash outside super. The process was really easy but I did need to break some TDs which took time (one required 30 days notice). My FA was willing to help with the process but I’m pretty confident Macquarie will help even without an FA involved so you should definitely approach them for some advice and help with the process.

[User #9015081749 postsranew68Whirlpool Enthusiast] flywire writes...
If you've ever left a job (even years ago), you'd meet a condition of release at 62 since you're over 60. Specifically, "ceasing an employment arrangement on or after age 60," allowing full super access without permanent retirement declaration or hour limits on your employment
Not true.
If you are retired it would be true, but you are still working part time. Retired is defined as "the person intends never again to become gainfully employed, whether on a full-time or part-time basis” (although less than 10 hours a week is generally taken to be consistent with “retired”).
If you are not retired the ceasing of the employment arrangement needs to be after you turned 60.
